title: Peculiar Pioneers — Ten Bible Studies
scope: Ten introductory topic studies with seven learning points each; selected passages, not an exhaustive course through every chapter.
editorialNote: All lesson explanations and flashcard answers are editorial summaries of the cited passages, not verbatim EGW quotations. Scripture memory texts are KJV; excerpts are identified. Dates and doctrinal explanations follow the cited EGW exposition. Reflection prompts are personal applications and are not scored.

topics.title: Righteousness by Faith
topics.description: Christ’s righteousness, assurance, living faith, and loving obedience.
topics.verseText: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.

items.title: The righteousness we cannot supply
items.reading: We cannot erase past sin or supply the righteousness God’s law requires by our own efforts. Christ lived a sinless life and died for us. He offers His righteousness to those who give themselves to Him and receive Him as their Saviour. Our hope begins with His provision.
items.reflect: What changes when you stop treating acceptance with God as something to earn?
items.flashQuestion: Why do sinners need Christ’s righteousness?
items.flashAnswer: We have no righteousness of our own that can meet the claims of God’s holy law.
items.question: What meets the sinner’s need for righteousness before God?

options.text: The righteousness provided by Jesus Christ.
options.feedback: We cannot erase past sin or supply the righteousness God’s law requires by our own efforts. Christ lived a sinless life and died for us. He offers His righteousness to those who give themselves to Him and receive Him as their Saviour. Our hope begins with His provision.

options.text: Religious effort sufficient to make Christ unnecessary.
options.feedback: The source identifies our need for Christ’s righteousness.

options.text: A comparison showing fewer sins than someone else.
options.feedback: The standard is God’s holy law, not another person’s record.

options.text: An improved reputation that erases the past.
options.feedback: A reputation cannot remove guilt or supply perfect righteousness.

items.hint: Review “The righteousness we cannot supply” and Romans 3:20–24.

items.title: Accepted in Christ
items.reading: When we surrender to Christ and accept Him, His character stands in place of ours, and we are accepted before God for His sake. This is no boast in personal merit. Justification gives peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ and directs all gratitude to Him.
items.reflect: How does acceptance for Christ’s sake answer both pride and despair?
items.flashQuestion: On whose righteousness does our acceptance with God depend?
items.flashAnswer: Christ’s righteousness; His character stands in place of ours.
items.question: What is the basis of acceptance described in Steps to Christ, page 62?

options.text: Our flawless performance before first approaching Him.
options.feedback: The invitation is to the sinner who gives himself to Christ and accepts Him.

options.text: Christ’s character and righteousness received by faith.
options.feedback: When we surrender to Christ and accept Him, His character stands in place of ours, and we are accepted before God for His sake. This is no boast in personal merit. Justification gives peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ and directs all gratitude to Him.

options.text: The approval of a respected religious person.
options.feedback: Acceptance rests in Christ, not another person’s approval.

options.text: Our ability to feel forgiven at every moment.
options.feedback: The foundation is Christ’s provision, not constant emotional certainty.

items.hint: Review “Accepted in Christ” and Romans 5:1.

items.title: Faith involves trust and surrender
items.reading: Acknowledging that God exists is not the same as saving faith. Steps to Christ describes faith that receives God’s Word, yields the will, and fixes the affections on Him. Such faith works by love and opens the life to His renewing power.
items.reflect: Where is God asking you to move from agreement into trust?
items.flashQuestion: How does living faith differ from intellectual assent?
items.flashAnswer: It trusts God, yields the will to Him, and works by love.
items.question: A person agrees with Bible facts but refuses to yield the will. What is still missing?

options.text: Nothing; agreement with facts is the whole of faith.
options.feedback: The source distinguishes factual assent from living faith.

options.text: Living trust and surrender to God.
options.feedback: Acknowledging that God exists is not the same as saving faith. Steps to Christ describes faith that receives God’s Word, yields the will, and fixes the affections on Him. Such faith works by love and opens the life to His renewing power.

options.text: Only more religious vocabulary.
options.feedback: The distinction concerns the will and heart, not vocabulary.

options.text: A stronger argument that even devils acknowledge God.
options.feedback: James uses that acknowledgment to show belief alone is insufficient.

items.hint: Review “Faith involves trust and surrender” and James 2:19–20.

items.title: Faith and God’s promise
items.reading: God invites us to confess, give ourselves to Him, and believe His promise of forgiveness. We need not wait for a particular feeling before trusting His word. Assurance rests in God’s faithfulness as we come to Him in repentance and faith, not in an emotional performance.
items.reflect: Which promise can you hold to when feelings are unsettled?
items.flashQuestion: Must we feel forgiven before believing God’s promise?
items.flashAnswer: No. We may trust His promise as we come in repentance and faith.
items.question: A repentant person has confessed but does not feel changed immediately. What does Steps to Christ counsel?

options.text: Assume unsettled emotions prove the confession was rejected.
options.feedback: Emotional state is not the standard of God’s faithfulness.

options.text: Trust God’s promise and continue yielding to Him.
options.feedback: God invites us to confess, give ourselves to Him, and believe His promise of forgiveness. We need not wait for a particular feeling before trusting His word. Assurance rests in God’s faithfulness as we come to Him in repentance and faith, not in an emotional performance.

options.text: Purchase assurance with a sufficient number of good deeds.
options.feedback: Forgiveness is received through Christ, not bought with deeds.

options.text: Wait for a special feeling before believing His word.
options.feedback: The chapter teaches trust in the promise rather than dependence on a feeling.

items.hint: Review “Faith and God’s promise” and 1 John 1:9.

items.title: The same Christ who pardons also renews
items.reading: Christ not only provides righteousness for our acceptance; He also changes the heart. As we remain connected to Him through faith and surrender, He works in us to will and to do His good pleasure. His grace produces love, obedience, and good works in the life.
items.reflect: What change would demonstrate Christ’s work within your ordinary relationships?
items.flashQuestion: What does Christ do beyond granting pardon?
items.flashAnswer: He changes the heart and works within us to produce willing obedience.
items.question: Which statement describes the work of Christ in the believer?

options.text: He leaves the believer to generate holiness independently.
options.feedback: He works within those who remain joined to Him.

options.text: He grants a label of righteousness while opposing all change.
options.feedback: Steps to Christ explicitly says Christ changes the heart.

options.text: He changes behavior only through pressure from other people.
options.feedback: The source describes His inward work through faith and surrender.

options.text: He provides acceptance and renews the heart for loving obedience.
options.feedback: Christ not only provides righteousness for our acceptance; He also changes the heart. As we remain connected to Him through faith and surrender, He works in us to will and to do His good pleasure. His grace produces love, obedience, and good works in the life.

items.hint: Review “The same Christ who pardons also renews” and Philippians 2:13.

items.title: Grace bears fruit in love
items.reading: Salvation is the free gift of God, received by faith. Obedience and service are its fruit. As love for Christ fills the heart, we desire to please Him and bless others. A living faith neither boasts in works nor uses grace to excuse disobedience.
items.reflect: What act of service could express gratitude for Christ’s grace this week?
items.flashQuestion: Where do obedience and service belong in righteousness by faith?
items.flashAnswer: They are the fruit of living faith and gratitude for grace, not the purchase price of salvation.
items.question: Which statement brings grace and obedience together correctly?

options.text: We purchase salvation through obedience, then add faith.
options.feedback: Ephesians places salvation in God’s gift of grace through faith.

options.text: Works matter chiefly because they give us grounds to boast.
options.feedback: The passage excludes boasting and directs gratitude to God.

options.text: Grace removes any purpose for good works.
options.feedback: Ephesians 2:10 describes a life created in Christ for good works.

options.text: We receive salvation by faith, and that living faith produces loving obedience.
options.feedback: Salvation is the free gift of God, received by faith. Obedience and service are its fruit. As love for Christ fills the heart, we desire to please Him and bless others. A living faith neither boasts in works nor uses grace to excuse disobedience.

items.hint: Review “Grace bears fruit in love” and Ephesians 2:8–10.

items.title: Rejoicing in the Lord
items.reading: Trust in Christ gives reason for gratitude and hope. Steps to Christ invites us to remember God’s mercies and represent His goodness to others. Christian joy does not mean that trials or tears disappear, or that feelings remain constantly bright. We may bring our cares to God and rest in His love while encouraging one another.
items.reflect: What mercy from God could you remember and share with someone today?
items.flashQuestion: How can faith in Christ support joy during trials?
items.flashAnswer: By resting in His love, remembering His mercies, and bringing our cares to Him.
items.question: Which response reflects rejoicing in the Lord during a difficult season?

options.text: Acknowledge the trial, bring it to God, and remember His faithful love.
options.feedback: Trust in Christ gives reason for gratitude and hope. Steps to Christ invites us to remember God’s mercies and represent His goodness to others. Christian joy does not mean that trials or tears disappear, or that feelings remain constantly bright. We may bring our cares to God and rest in His love while encouraging one another.

options.text: Pretend that grief or difficulty does not exist.
options.feedback: Christian hope does not require denying real trials or tears.

options.text: Focus only on past failures and exclude every memory of mercy.
options.feedback: Steps to Christ calls attention to God’s promises and the evidences of His care.

options.text: Treat a sad feeling as proof that Christ has rejected you.
options.feedback: Assurance rests in Christ’s faithfulness, not an unbroken feeling of happiness.

items.hint: Review “Rejoicing in the Lord” and Romans 5:1–2,11.

topics.title: Victory Over Sin
topics.description: Repentance, surrender, abiding in Christ, and a changed life.
topics.verseText: For without me ye can do nothing.

items.title: Repentance reaches the heart
items.reading: True repentance includes sorrow for sin and turning away from it. It goes deeper than fear of punishment. Christ draws us to Himself and gives the repentance we cannot produce by our own strength. David sought a clean heart as well as pardon.
items.reflect: Is there a wrong you have regretted mainly because of its consequences?
items.flashQuestion: What distinguishes true repentance from regret over consequences?
items.flashAnswer: Sorrow for sin itself and a turning away from it, through Christ’s grace.
items.question: Which response most clearly expresses true repentance?

options.text: Regret being discovered while planning to repeat the wrong.
options.feedback: Regret over consequences is not a turning away from sin.

options.text: Blame circumstances so personal guilt can be avoided.
options.feedback: Repentance honestly acknowledges the wrong.

options.text: Ask God for a clean heart and turn from the sin itself.
options.feedback: True repentance includes sorrow for sin and turning away from it. It goes deeper than fear of punishment. Christ draws us to Himself and gives the repentance we cannot produce by our own strength. David sought a clean heart as well as pardon.

options.text: Wait to become worthy before coming to Christ.
options.feedback: Christ Himself draws us and gives repentance.

items.hint: Review “Repentance reaches the heart” and Acts 3:19.

items.title: Yielding the will
items.reading: We cannot change the heart by unaided effort, but we can choose to yield our will to God. As we surrender to Christ, He works within us to will and to do His pleasure. Victory involves real choice and cooperation with His power, not passive permission for sin to continue.
items.reflect: What decision can you consciously place under Christ’s direction today?
items.flashQuestion: What can we choose when we cannot change our own hearts?
items.flashAnswer: Yield our will to Christ and depend on His transforming power.
items.question: Which response follows the counsel on the will in Steps to Christ?

options.text: Assume surrender means making no choices against sin.
options.feedback: Surrender is an active choice to place the will under God.

options.text: Expect willpower alone to regenerate the heart.
options.feedback: The heart’s renewal requires Christ’s power.

options.text: Wait until every desire changes before choosing God.
options.feedback: We may choose to yield while depending on Him to change the desires.

options.text: Choose to yield to Christ and cooperate with His working within.
options.feedback: We cannot change the heart by unaided effort, but we can choose to yield our will to God. As we surrender to Christ, He works within us to will and to do His pleasure. Victory involves real choice and cooperation with His power, not passive permission for sin to continue.

items.hint: Review “Yielding the will” and James 4:7–8.

items.title: Abiding in Christ
items.reading: A branch bears fruit by remaining joined to the vine. In the same way, a holy life depends continually on Christ. Daily consecration, trust, and communion sustain this relationship. Growth is not achieved by a moment of surrender followed by independence from Him.
items.reflect: What could make daily consecration a real practice rather than a phrase?
items.flashQuestion: What does the vine and branches illustration teach about victory?
items.flashAnswer: We depend continually on union with Christ for a fruitful, holy life.
items.question: Why does the branch bear fruit in John 15?

options.text: It becomes independent of the vine after its first growth.
options.feedback: Jesus teaches continuing dependence.

options.text: It abides in the vine and receives life from it.
options.feedback: A branch bears fruit by remaining joined to the vine. In the same way, a holy life depends continually on Christ. Daily consecration, trust, and communion sustain this relationship. Growth is not achieved by a moment of surrender followed by independence from Him.

options.text: It avoids any connection so growth will be entirely its own.
options.feedback: Apart from the vine the branch cannot bear fruit.

options.text: It produces life by trying to look like other branches.
options.feedback: Life comes from union with the vine, not comparison.

items.hint: Review “Abiding in Christ” and John 15:4–5.

items.title: Watch, pray, and take the way of escape
items.reading: Jesus calls us to watch and pray against temptation. Scripture promises God’s faithfulness and a way of escape. We are to rely on His help and act on the light He gives: treasure His Word, turn from the tempting course, and seek grace in the moment of need.
items.reflect: What practical escape could you prepare for a recurring temptation?
items.flashQuestion: What response to temptation joins faith with action?
items.flashAnswer: Watch and pray, rely on God’s help, and take the way of escape He provides.
items.question: A familiar temptation appears. Which response best follows these passages?

options.text: Remain in the temptation to prove personal strength.
options.feedback: Watchfulness does not require deliberately staying in avoidable temptation.

options.text: Treat prayer as a substitute for responding to God’s guidance.
options.feedback: The counsel joins prayer and watchfulness with obedient action.

options.text: Assume temptation makes yielding unavoidable.
options.feedback: God promises help and a way of escape.

options.text: Pray for help and act on the available way of escape.
options.feedback: Jesus calls us to watch and pray against temptation. Scripture promises God’s faithfulness and a way of escape. We are to rely on His help and act on the light He gives: treasure His Word, turn from the tempting course, and seek grace in the moment of need.

items.hint: Review “Watch, pray, and take the way of escape” and Matthew 26:41.

items.title: When a believer falls
items.reading: God calls us away from sin; if we fall, we have an Advocate in Jesus Christ. Confess the particular wrong, forsake it, and return to Him. Steps to Christ counsels against despair while also rejecting excuses for sin. His mercy invites renewed repentance and trust.
items.reflect: How can you respond to failure without either excusing it or giving up?
items.flashQuestion: What should a believer do after falling into sin?
items.flashAnswer: Confess and forsake the sin, returning in faith to Christ our Advocate.
items.question: After a failure, which response holds together mercy and repentance?

options.text: Acknowledge the wrong, forsake it, and return to Jesus.
options.feedback: God calls us away from sin; if we fall, we have an Advocate in Jesus Christ. Confess the particular wrong, forsake it, and return to Him. Steps to Christ counsels against despair while also rejecting excuses for sin. His mercy invites renewed repentance and trust.

options.text: Conclude that Christ will never receive a returning sinner.
options.feedback: The passages offer forgiveness and advocacy to the repentant.

options.text: Use forgiveness as permission to plan the same sin again.
options.feedback: Mercy calls us away from sin, not into a plan to continue it.

options.text: Hide the wrong to preserve a religious appearance.
options.feedback: Concealment prevents honest confession and repentance.

items.hint: Review “When a believer falls” and 1 John 1:9.

items.title: Real growth without self-exaltation
items.reading: Sanctification is the work of God’s Word and Spirit in the life. It is lifelong growth in Christlike character, involving daily surrender and obedience. The closer we come to Jesus, the more clearly we see our need of His grace. Real victory does not make us independent of Christ or give us grounds for boasting.
items.reflect: What evidence of grace can you recognize without claiming credit for it?
items.flashQuestion: How should growth in holiness affect our attitude?
items.flashAnswer: It should deepen dependence on Christ and humility while producing real obedience.
items.question: Which statement best describes sanctification in these sources?

options.text: Success that makes Christ’s daily help unnecessary.
options.feedback: Spiritual growth increases our awareness of dependence on Him.

options.text: A claim of holiness that ends the need for growth.
options.feedback: The sources present continuing growth, not self-satisfied finality.

options.text: An unchanged life protected by religious language.
options.feedback: Sanctification changes the character and conduct.

options.text: Lifelong growth in holiness through God’s Word and Spirit, with humble dependence on Christ.
options.feedback: Sanctification is the work of God’s Word and Spirit in the life. It is lifelong growth in Christlike character, involving daily surrender and obedience. The closer we come to Jesus, the more clearly we see our need of His grace. Real victory does not make us independent of Christ or give us grounds for boasting.

items.hint: Review “Real growth without self-exaltation” and John 17:17.

items.title: Learning Christ’s character
items.reading: Steps to Christ directs us to contemplate Jesus’ love and character, copy His example, and depend on Him. John’s naturally resentful and ambitious temper was changed as he followed his Master and yielded to His influence. The Holy Spirit works real transformation as our attention and affections are fixed on Christ.
items.reflect: Which trait in Jesus’ character would you like to study and imitate more closely?
items.flashQuestion: How was John’s character changed as he followed Jesus?
items.flashAnswer: He beheld Christ’s character, yielded to Him, and was renewed by the Holy Spirit.
items.question: What does John’s experience in Steps to Christ illustrate?

options.text: Christ’s love and the Holy Spirit can transform a yielded person’s character.
options.feedback: Steps to Christ directs us to contemplate Jesus’ love and character, copy His example, and depend on Him. John’s naturally resentful and ambitious temper was changed as he followed his Master and yielded to His influence. The Holy Spirit works real transformation as our attention and affections are fixed on Christ.

options.text: Admiring Jesus from a distance made surrender unnecessary.
options.feedback: John yielded his temper to the molding power of Christ.

options.text: Remembering personal defects alone supplies the power to change.
options.feedback: The chapter directs attention to Christ as the source of strength and transformation.

options.text: John naturally possessed every Christlike trait without needing change.
options.feedback: The chapter describes his former ambition and resentment and his need of renewal.

items.hint: Review “Learning Christ’s character” and 2 Corinthians 3:18.

topics.title: The Law of God
topics.description: God’s character, the knowledge of sin, and loving obedience.
topics.verseText: Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.

items.title: A revelation of God’s character
items.reading: God’s law is holy, just, and good. Ellen White describes it as a revelation of His will and character, embodying the principle of love. Its authority rests in who God is, rather than in changing human custom or preference.
items.reflect: How does seeing the law as an expression of God’s character change your response?
items.flashQuestion: How does Romans 7:12 describe the law?
items.flashAnswer: Holy, just, and good.
items.question: Which description agrees with Romans 7:12?

options.text: The law is merely an unreliable human tradition.
options.feedback: The passage treats it as God’s holy commandment.

options.text: The law becomes good only when a majority approves it.
options.feedback: Its goodness rests in God, not popular approval.

options.text: The law is the cause of God’s moral imperfection.
options.feedback: Paul affirms the law’s goodness, not moral defect in God.

options.text: The law is holy, just, and good.
options.feedback: God’s law is holy, just, and good. Ellen White describes it as a revelation of His will and character, embodying the principle of love. Its authority rests in who God is, rather than in changing human custom or preference.

items.hint: Review “A revelation of God’s character” and Romans 7:12.

items.title: The knowledge of sin
items.reading: The law makes sin known. Like a mirror, it reveals the condition that needs correction, but it cannot supply forgiveness or change the heart by itself. Conviction should lead the sinner to Christ for pardon and renewal.
items.reflect: What should you do when Scripture makes a fault clear?
items.flashQuestion: What does the law make known according to Romans 3:20?
items.flashAnswer: The knowledge of sin.
items.question: If the law reveals a person’s guilt, what further need remains?

options.text: Christ’s forgiveness and renewing grace.
options.feedback: The law makes sin known. Like a mirror, it reveals the condition that needs correction, but it cannot supply forgiveness or change the heart by itself. Conviction should lead the sinner to Christ for pardon and renewal.

options.text: Enough comparison with others to feel superior.
options.feedback: Comparison cannot cleanse guilt or renew the heart.

options.text: No further need; recognizing guilt itself removes it.
options.feedback: A mirror reveals a problem but does not remove it; conviction is not pardon.

options.text: A new standard that declares the same sin acceptable.
options.feedback: Changing the standard does not reconcile the sinner to God.

items.hint: Review “The knowledge of sin” and Romans 3:20.

items.title: Love is the governing principle
items.reading: Jesus gathers the law’s claims into love to God and love to our neighbor. Love does not authorize harm or disobedience; it expresses the purpose of the commandments. When God renews the heart, love becomes the motive for a life in harmony with His will.
items.reflect: Which commandment can you connect with a concrete act of love?
items.flashQuestion: What two loves summarize the law and the prophets?
items.flashAnswer: Love to God with the whole heart, and love to our neighbor as ourselves.
items.question: How does love relate to God’s commandments?

options.text: Love means outward compliance without concern for people.
options.feedback: The commandments are fulfilled from a heart governed by love.

options.text: Love permits harm whenever intentions feel sincere.
options.feedback: Biblical love does no ill to the neighbor.

options.text: Love fulfills their purpose through faithfulness to God and care for others.
options.feedback: Jesus gathers the law’s claims into love to God and love to our neighbor. Love does not authorize harm or disobedience; it expresses the purpose of the commandments. When God renews the heart, love becomes the motive for a life in harmony with His will.

options.text: Love removes any need for an obedient life.
options.feedback: Love fulfills the law rather than making disobedience harmless.

items.hint: Review “Love is the governing principle” and Matthew 22:37–40.

items.title: Christ upheld God’s law
items.reading: Jesus said He came to fulfill, not destroy, the law and the prophets. He lived in obedience to His Father. The ceremonial sacrifices met their fulfillment in His death; this does not mean the Ten Commandments ceased to reveal God’s moral will.
items.reflect: How does Christ’s example help you understand obedience?
items.flashQuestion: Did Christ’s fulfillment make God’s moral law void?
items.flashAnswer: No. He upheld it and lived in obedience; the sacrificial types found their fulfillment in His death.
items.question: Which distinction helps explain Christ’s fulfillment?

options.text: Sacrificial types met their fulfillment in His death; God’s moral law remains.
options.feedback: Jesus said He came to fulfill, not destroy, the law and the prophets. He lived in obedience to His Father. The ceremonial sacrifices met their fulfillment in His death; this does not mean the Ten Commandments ceased to reveal God’s moral will.

options.text: Every moral command ended with the animal sacrifices.
options.feedback: The end of sacrificial types is not the abolition of the moral law.

options.text: Christ fulfilled the law by violating its principles.
options.feedback: Jesus testified that He kept His Father’s commandments.

options.text: The cross means sin can no longer be identified.
options.feedback: God’s law continues to reveal sin and His holy character.

items.hint: Review “Christ upheld God’s law” and Matthew 5:17–19.

items.title: Written in the heart
items.reading: The new covenant promises God’s law within the heart. God gives a new heart and His Spirit, enabling obedience from within. The change reaches motives, affections, and conduct, producing more than outward agreement with religious expectations.
items.reflect: What motive would you like God to renew within you?
items.flashQuestion: Where does God promise to write His law under the new covenant?
items.flashAnswer: In the hearts and minds of His people.
items.question: What change does the new-covenant promise describe?

options.text: The erasure of all moral responsibility.
options.feedback: God writes His law within; He does not erase its principles.

options.text: Only a change of religious label.
options.feedback: The promise concerns the inner life, not a label alone.

options.text: God writes His law within and renews the heart for obedience.
options.feedback: The new covenant promises God’s law within the heart. God gives a new heart and His Spirit, enabling obedience from within. The change reaches motives, affections, and conduct, producing more than outward agreement with religious expectations.

options.text: External pressure without any change in desire.
options.feedback: The promise includes a new heart and the Spirit’s work.

items.hint: Review “Written in the heart” and Hebrews 10:16.

items.title: Obedience as the fruit of faith
items.reading: We are saved by grace through faith, not by earning God’s favor through works. Yet faith in Christ brings a changed life. Ellen White warns against both trusting works to save and claiming that belief makes obedience unnecessary. Christ gives pardon and power for a life of good works.
items.reflect: How can you pursue obedience while resting in Christ’s acceptance?
items.flashQuestion: What is the relationship between salvation, faith, and obedience?
items.flashAnswer: Salvation is God’s gift received by faith; obedience is the fruit of that living faith.
items.question: Which statement avoids the two errors identified in Steps to Christ?

options.text: Faith frees a believer to disregard God’s law.
options.feedback: Living faith receives grace that enables obedience.

options.text: Outward conformity is enough without a renewed heart.
options.feedback: God seeks the obedience of love from a renewed heart.

options.text: Trust Christ for salvation and let living faith bear the fruit of obedience.
options.feedback: We are saved by grace through faith, not by earning God’s favor through works. Yet faith in Christ brings a changed life. Ellen White warns against both trusting works to save and claiming that belief makes obedience unnecessary. Christ gives pardon and power for a life of good works.

options.text: Good conduct can purchase God’s acceptance.
options.feedback: Salvation is the gift of grace, not a wage earned by conduct.

items.hint: Review “Obedience as the fruit of faith” and Ephesians 2:8–10.

items.title: The perfect law of liberty
items.reading: James calls God’s law the perfect law of liberty, and the psalmist connects liberty with seeking God’s precepts. Sin is bondage; Christ makes us free to live in harmony with God. Christian freedom is therefore not permission to injure others or disregard His will. It is a life of willing allegiance to our Redeemer.
items.reflect: How has obedience to a good principle protected freedom in your life?
items.flashQuestion: What does James call the law in James 1:25?
items.flashAnswer: The perfect law of liberty.
items.question: Which understanding of freedom agrees with these passages?

options.text: Freedom is the unrestricted right to harm a neighbor.
options.feedback: Such conduct is bondage to sin, not the liberty described here.

options.text: Christ frees us from sin’s bondage for willing obedience to God.
options.feedback: James calls God’s law the perfect law of liberty, and the psalmist connects liberty with seeking God’s precepts. Sin is bondage; Christ makes us free to live in harmony with God. Christian freedom is therefore not permission to injure others or disregard His will. It is a life of willing allegiance to our Redeemer.

options.text: Freedom means God’s moral will no longer matters.
options.feedback: James calls the law a law of liberty, and Christ frees people from sin.

options.text: Freedom is achieved by replacing Christ with personal merit.
options.feedback: John 8 identifies the Son as the One who makes us free.

items.hint: Review “The perfect law of liberty” and James 1:25.

topics.title: The Sabbath
topics.description: Creation, the seventh day, joyful worship, and the works of mercy.
topics.verseText: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.

items.title: A gift from Creation
items.reading: God rested on the seventh day, blessed it, and sanctified it at Creation. The Sabbath was given for humanity’s good before Israel existed as a nation. It is a memorial of the Creator’s power and love, calling us to remember the One who made us.
items.reflect: What does the Sabbath teach you about your value as God’s creation?
items.flashQuestion: When did God bless and sanctify the seventh day?
items.flashAnswer: At Creation, when He rested after His work of making the world.
items.question: Where does Scripture first locate the blessing and sanctifying of the seventh day?

options.text: At the resurrection of Jesus.
options.feedback: The seventh day was sanctified in Genesis, long before the resurrection.

options.text: At the giving of the manna in the wilderness.
options.feedback: The manna instruction came later; Genesis already records the blessing.

options.text: At Solomon’s dedication of the temple.
options.feedback: The Sabbath precedes the temple and Israel’s monarchy.

options.text: At the completion of Creation.
options.feedback: God rested on the seventh day, blessed it, and sanctified it at Creation. The Sabbath was given for humanity’s good before Israel existed as a nation. It is a memorial of the Creator’s power and love, calling us to remember the One who made us.

items.question: What purpose does Ephesians 4 assign to the gifts, including prophets?

options.text: Keeping spiritual knowledge within a privileged circle.
options.feedback: The gifts equip the saints for ministry and build up the body.

options.text: Making one gifted person the center of Christian worship.
options.feedback: The gifts serve Christ’s body and do not transfer worship to a person.

options.text: Ending the need for believers to grow.
options.feedback: The stated aim is growth toward Christlike maturity.

options.text: Equipping and building up the church toward maturity in Christ.
options.feedback: Christ gives spiritual gifts, including prophets, to equip believers, build up His church, and bring them toward maturity in Him. Ellen White explains that the Spirit’s enlightening, warning, and comforting work continues after the close of the biblical canon. Spiritual gifts serve the body of Christ.

items.hint: Review “Gifts for the building up of the church” and Ephesians 4:11–13.

items.title: Scripture remains the standard
items.reading: Ellen White identifies the Bible as the standard of character, doctrine, and experience. The Holy Spirit inspired Scripture and does not teach against it. His continuing guidance opens and applies the Word. Genuine spiritual counsel strengthens our attention to Scripture.
items.reflect: How can you read an EGW passage together with its Bible foundation?
items.flashQuestion: What standard did Ellen White give for doctrine and spiritual experience?
items.flashAnswer: The Holy Scriptures.
items.question: A teacher claims the Spirit has made Bible study unnecessary. How does GC vii respond?

options.text: Private impressions become the final test of truth.
options.feedback: GC vii warns against impressions that neglect Scripture.

options.text: The Spirit illuminates Scripture and never supersedes its authority.
options.feedback: Ellen White identifies the Bible as the standard of character, doctrine, and experience. The Holy Spirit inspired Scripture and does not teach against it. His continuing guidance opens and applies the Word. Genuine spiritual counsel strengthens our attention to Scripture.

options.text: Popularity establishes whether a doctrine is inspired.
options.feedback: The stated standard is Scripture, not popularity.

options.text: Prophetic counsel may contradict the Bible when circumstances change.
options.feedback: The Spirit who inspired Scripture does not teach contrary to it.

items.hint: Review “Scripture remains the standard” and 2 Timothy 3:16–17.

items.title: Test the spirits
items.reading: Do not accept every spiritual claim. Test teaching by Scripture, examine its confession of Jesus Christ, and consider its fruit. Wonders and strong impressions cannot settle the question. The Bible supplies safeguards against false teachers and deceptive manifestations.
items.reflect: Which test would you apply before sharing a dramatic spiritual claim?
items.flashQuestion: Name biblical tests for a claimed prophetic message.
items.flashAnswer: Agreement with Scripture, confession of Jesus Christ, and the fruit of the teaching and life.
items.question: Which approach uses the biblical tests of a spiritual claim?

options.text: Examine Scripture agreement, its confession of Christ, and its fruit.
options.feedback: Do not accept every spiritual claim. Test teaching by Scripture, examine its confession of Jesus Christ, and consider its fruit. Wonders and strong impressions cannot settle the question. The Bible supplies safeguards against false teachers and deceptive manifestations.

options.text: Accept it if a remarkable prediction appears accurate.
options.feedback: A striking prediction alone is not the full biblical test.

options.text: Reject examination because testing shows unbelief.
options.feedback: John explicitly instructs believers to try the spirits.

options.text: Accept it if the speaker attracts a large audience.
options.feedback: Audience size does not prove divine inspiration.

items.hint: Review “Test the spirits” and 1 John 4:1–3.

items.title: A receptive and discerning response
items.reading: Paul joins openness to prophetic counsel with careful examination: believers are to prove all things and hold fast what is good. Ellen White likewise warns against both neglecting the Spirit’s work and following impressions apart from Scripture. Study prayerfully and test faithfully.
items.reflect: Which is harder for you: listening willingly or examining carefully?
items.flashQuestion: How does 1 Thessalonians 5 balance openness and discernment?
items.flashAnswer: Do not despise prophesyings; prove all things and hold fast what is good.
items.question: Which response follows Paul’s counsel about prophesyings?

options.text: Accept every claim without examining it.
options.feedback: Paul commands believers to prove all things.

options.text: Listen without contempt, examine the claim, and hold fast what is good.
options.feedback: Paul joins openness to prophetic counsel with careful examination: believers are to prove all things and hold fast what is good. Ellen White likewise warns against both neglecting the Spirit’s work and following impressions apart from Scripture. Study prayerfully and test faithfully.

options.text: Keep whichever claim best matches personal preference.
options.feedback: The test concerns what is good and true, not preference.

options.text: Dismiss all prophetic counsel without reading it.
options.feedback: Paul also says not to despise prophesyings.

items.hint: Review “A receptive and discerning response” and 1 Thessalonians 5:19–21.

items.title: Why Ellen White presented the controversy
items.reading: In her introduction, Ellen White describes the Spirit opening to her the conflict between Christ and Satan. She explains her purpose in presenting these scenes: to expose deception, make the issues of the conflict clear, and help people stand faithfully before the Lord. Read that account alongside her instruction to test teaching by Scripture.
items.reflect: How should learning about the controversy change daily faithfulness?
items.flashQuestion: What purpose did Ellen White give for presenting the great controversy?
items.flashAnswer: To clarify the conflict, uncover deception, and help people prepare to stand faithfully before Christ.
items.question: Which use of The Great Controversy matches its author’s stated purpose?

options.text: Study its warnings and principles to follow Christ faithfully.
options.feedback: In her introduction, Ellen White describes the Spirit opening to her the conflict between Christ and Satan. She explains her purpose in presenting these scenes: to expose deception, make the issues of the conflict clear, and help people stand faithfully before the Lord. Read that account alongside her instruction to test teaching by Scripture.

options.text: Use its warnings to calculate an undisclosed date for Christ’s return.
options.feedback: The stated purpose is faithful preparation, not inventing a new date.

options.text: Treat it as permission to neglect the biblical standard.
options.feedback: Her introduction explicitly upholds Scripture’s authority.

options.feedback: Her stated aim extends to understanding the conflict and preparing for what lies ahead.

items.title: Study a passage in its context
items.reading: Careful study seeks the meaning of a passage and its relationship to the plan of salvation. Steps to Christ values thoughtful understanding above hasty reading. When reading Bible texts or EGW counsel, examine the surrounding explanation, compare the biblical teaching, and ask what the author is actually addressing before applying the words.
items.reflect: Which familiar quotation would you like to read in its full setting?
items.flashQuestion: What helps us use a passage faithfully?
items.flashAnswer: Read its context, understand its meaning, and compare its application with Scripture.
items.question: You find a striking quotation in a short post. What is the sound next step?

options.text: Assume popularity has already settled its meaning.
options.feedback: Careful understanding requires examination, not reliance on popularity.

options.text: Share it immediately if it agrees with your existing view.
options.feedback: Agreement with a preference does not establish that the quotation is being used faithfully.

options.text: Treat the shortest possible excerpt as the most reliable explanation.
options.feedback: An excerpt can omit qualifications or the subject being addressed.

options.text: Read the surrounding passage and check the proposed application against Scripture.
